articles.title: A 17-Million-Line Proof Says Yes. Here Is What It
articles.excerpt: On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, written with Claude, as a Lean library of about 17 million lines. A day later the Lean and Mathlib communities certified…
articles.body: On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, written with Claude, as a Lean library of about 17 million lines. A day later the Lean and Mathlib communities certified both its statement and its proof. Clay's prize still needs publication and time, but as a machine-checked result the question is answered: every nontrivial zero of ζ(s) lies on the line Re(s) = ½. A proof is a finite object. Lean does not walk the zeros one by one. It checks that every step follows from the last. So this post is not a complaint about size. It asks a different question, one a proof does not answer by itself: If a zero had left the line, how long would it take to notice? The twin Map each zero ρ through w = (ρ − 1)/ρ. On the critical line |w| = 1 exactly.

articles.title: AI Hallucination in Specs: The 15-Minute Claim Trace Audit
articles.excerpt: AI-written specs sound sourced but often aren't. The Claim Trace is a 15-minute audit that labels every claim Sourced, Inferred, Assumed or Invented before engineering or a coding agent builds from it…
articles.body: AI-written specs sound sourced but often aren't. The Claim Trace is a 15-minute audit that labels every claim Sourced, Inferred, Assumed or Invented before engineering or a coding agent builds from it. AI hallucination in specs is when an AI-written PRD or spec states something about your users, market or product that no source supports, in the same confident voice as the parts that are true. The fix is a short audit before anyone builds: trace every claim and label it Sourced, Inferred, Assumed or Invented. We call that audit the Claim Trace , and it takes about 15 minutes. Key takeaways NIST lists "confabulation" as one of 12 risks unique to or made worse by generative AI, and warns that models can also produce made-up citations that justify a wrong answer ( NIST, 2024 ).

articles.title: Node.js Signed Uploads for Expiring Support Documents (with Private Object Storage)
articles.excerpt: A signed customer-support document can be available for 30 days and still need to disappear at a precise deadline. That requirement changes the design. I would keep the object private, give each docum…
articles.body: A signed customer-support document can be available for 30 days and still need to disappear at a precise deadline. That requirement changes the design. I would keep the object private, give each document a unique key, store its deletion deadline in Postgres, and issue short-lived signed URLs for transfer. The Node.js application remains the authority on who may read the file and when deletion is due. TL;DR: use a signed browser upload only when the bucket's existing CORS policy already accepts your origin. Otherwise, proxy the bytes through Node.js. In both cases, treat URL expiry and document retention as separate clocks. The app owns the exact deletion deadline; a storage lifecycle rule, where available, is only a daily backstop.

articles.title: AI Automation for Product Managers: What to Automate, Assist and Own
articles.excerpt: A practical framework for AI automation in product management: which PM tasks to automate, which to assist, which to keep human-owned, and how to run a four-week pilot. AI automation for product manag…
articles.body: A practical framework for AI automation in product management: which PM tasks to automate, which to assist, which to keep human-owned, and how to run a four-week pilot. AI automation for product managers works best on repetitive, source-based work that a person can check in minutes: research synthesis, first drafts, status preparation, feedback triage and decision-log upkeep. It works badly on problem selection, prioritisation, customer interpretation and trade-offs. Sort every recurring task into one of three lanes, automate, assist or own, and automate the effort around judgment, never the judgment itself. Key takeaways Product people spend 27% of their time on strategic work but say it should be 53% (Pragmatic Institute, 2,474 respondents). That gap is what automation should close.

articles.excerpt: You signed up for your first hackathon. Now it's two days away and the panic has set in. Everyone else seems to already have a team, a plan, and probably a working prototype in their head already. Dee…
articles.body: You signed up for your first hackathon. Now it's two days away and the panic has set in. Everyone else seems to already have a team, a plan, and probably a working prototype in their head already. Deep breath. Nobody walks in fully ready, and the people who look calm are usually just better at hiding the same nerves you have. This is everything I wish someone had told me before my first one. 1. A Hackathon Is a Road Trip, Not a Race to a Finish Line Here's the mental shift that helps most. A hackathon isn't really a race where the fastest typist wins. It's closer to a road trip with a hard deadline: you don't need the fastest car, you need a decent plan, someone to read the map, and the sense to stop for gas before you run empty.

articles.body: On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center and up into the dark of night. This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall. Discovery had five astronauts on board. Their mission was to deploy a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. NASA and the military launched several secretive shuttle missions to deploy military satellites . The satellite that launched with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum. But exactly what Magnum was doing in orbit remains classified. articles.title: 10 things that worry me about chasing the 2027 total solar eclipse in Egypt
articles.excerpt: The longest total solar eclipse on land this century promises to be the experience of a lifetime, but watching it from Luxor, Egypt, may not be straightforward. What could go wrong? Quite a lot, actua…
articles.body: On Aug. 2, 2027, I'll be in Luxor, Egypt, to witness what could be the greatest total solar eclipse of my life. I've seen nine total solar eclipses across the world, but this one promises to be different. For a remarkable six minutes and 22 seconds, the moon will completely cover the sun, plunging Egypt's ancient temples and monuments into eerie twilight as the solar corona bursts into view. I've been calling it the "eclipse of the century" for many years, and for good reason. It will be the longest total solar eclipse until 2114 — and the longest on land of the 21st century — and it will take place in one of the most extraordinary places on Earth. What could go wrong? I've chased eclipses long enough to know that the celestial mechanics are the easy part.
